items.q: Was this a clean experiment on added sugar alone?
items.a: **No. Multiple variables changed together.** The controlled participant removed added sugar, refined starches, snacks, and many rich sauces; the comparison participant ate more sugar **and about 900 g more fat**. It is an illustrative self-experiment, not causal proof.

items.q: What body-composition changes were reported after 14 days?
items.a: The controlled-diet participant reportedly **lost 2 kg, including 0.8 kg fat**, while the high-sugar participant **gained 1.1 kg**. Their visceral-fat indices changed by **-5 versus +5.2**.

items.q: Why can “less sugar” or “no added sugar” drink labels mislead?
items.a: Sweetness settings do not necessarily scale linearly with total sugar. The tested fruit drink labeled no added sugar still contained about **4.28 g/100 ml**, or nearly **18 g in a 400+ ml serving**.

items.q: Why did the controlled diet also remove white rice?
items.a: **Refined starch is rapidly broken into glucose.** It may contain no added sugar yet still produce a sharp glucose rise. Pairing grains with fiber can slow absorption, but this also means the challenge tested more than sugar removal.

items.q: How did sweet-food cravings change during the challenge?
items.a: Cravings intensified early when habitual reward was removed, then reportedly weakened after roughly **ten days**. That pattern is compatible with adaptation, but one participant cannot establish a universal timeline.

items.q: Did removing sugar prove that skin would improve?
items.a: **No.** Skin imaging and self-reports suggested less redness, oiliness, and new acne in the controlled group, but skincare, stress, sleep, total diet, and natural variation were uncontrolled. The creators explicitly call the challenge non-rigorous.

items.q: What does the nutritionist mean by a “small cut” strategy?
items.a: Make **one manageable reduction at a time**: for example, move from full-sugar to half-sugar milk tea for a week before making another change. This avoids turning a useful reduction into an unsustainable all-or-nothing rule.

items.q: What is the most defensible conclusion from the video?
items.a: **Track the whole dietary change, not just the sugar label.** Liquid sugar, refined starch, fat, fiber, portions, and adherence all matter. Use the video to generate a testable personal habit, not to claim that 14 sugar-free days guarantee its reported results.
